title: Scientific Talent Leaks Out of Funding Gaps
authors: Wei Yang Tham; Joseph Staudt; Elisabeth Ruth Perlman; Stephanie Cheng
abstract: Abstract Federal research funding is a key input into scientific work, but funding streams can be disrupted. We study how delays in renewed NIH research grants affect lab personnel’s careers, linking grant records to university payroll, tax, Census, and publication data. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that interruptions of at least 30 days increase nonemployment among personnel in labs supported by a single NIH R01 grant by 3 percentage points, or 40%. Among those who remain employed in the US, earnings decrease by 20%. The results show that short funding gaps can alter career trajectories, especially for trainees.

title: The Dynamics of Social Insurance in Egypt
abstract: ABSTRACT Social insurance coverage is low and declining in Egypt. This paper uses panel data, spanning 1998–2023, to assess the dynamics behind these trends in social insurance coverage. The results highlight not only the decline of social insurance coverage but an informality trap: over time workers are less likely to gain social insurance at entry or while remaining employed, and they are increasingly likely to lose social insurance. One reason for the decline in social insurance may be the low value workers place on coverage; the unemployed average the same reservation wages for jobs with and without social insurance coverage.

title: Anticipatory Fertility
authors: Anna Bárdits; Anna Adamecz; Márta Bisztray; Andrea Weber; Ágnes Szabó‐Morvai
abstract: Abstract We study fertility responses to employment shocks using unique Hungarian administrative data linking firm-level mass layoff and closure events to individual-level birth and abortion records. We show that the main fertility response occurs in anticipation and differs by shock type. The number of conceptions leading to births increases in the year preceding a mass layoff (when maternal employment protection is available), but not before a firm closure (without employment protection). We interpret this result as evidence of anticipatory fertility behavior: women tend to schedule childbirth when job loss can be avoided.

title: How do misperceptions about non-monetary and monetary aspects of government jobs influence bureaucratic selection?
authors: Bo Feng; Qiwei He; Hanzhang Liu
abstract: This paper investigates how misperceptions about non-monetary and monetary aspects of government jobs affect individuals’ propensity to choose civil service as a career in China. Based on a survey sample of more than 2,000 college students in China, we document the prevalence of misperceptions about government jobs in terms of promotion prospects, salary compensation, and housing benefits. When misperceptions are corrected using a survey experiment, we find that individuals who overestimate (underestimate) promotion prospects, salary compensation, and housing benefits significantly decrease (increase) their interest in government jobs; the effects of these corrections are asymmetric based on respondents’ prior misperceptions. Moreover, we find that those who are more prosocial increase (decrease) their interest in government jobs more than others, when their underestimation (overestimation) of promotion prospects is corrected. These results point to the significant impact of individuals’ (mis)perceptions about government jobs on bureaucratic selection, especially in terms of non-monetary aspects such as career prospects.

title: Attention to the Macroeconomy
authors: Sebastian Link; Andreas Peichl; Oliver Pfäuti; Christopher Roth; Johannes Wohlfart
abstract: Abstract We measure which economic topics are top of mind using quarterly German household and firm panels from 2020 to 2024, a period that spans the post-pandemic inflation surge and the subsequent disinflation. With these data, we study potential determinants and consequences of having inflation top of mind. In line with goal-directed attention, the likelihood that inflation is top of mind rises with proxies for its true payoff relevance. At the same time, prior experiences predict whether respondents have inflation and energy prices top of mind conditional on a large set of controls for payoff relevance, and this relationship strengthens when the environment becomes more inflationary. Having inflation top of mind predicts stronger increases in information acquisition and inflation expectations over the shock period. At odds with goal-optimality, having inflation top of mind is associated with expectations further away from multiple ex-ante benchmarks. Finally, both key determinants of having inflation top of mind—payoff relevance and prior experiences—are associated with stronger shifts of expectations away from these benchmarks over the shock period.
